operations.name: Leah Young

expected.name: Leah Young
expected.description: Leah Young was an Atlanta textile worker and the sister of fellow striker Annie Mae Leathers. Born and raised in Georgia, she began working at eight and was working twelve-hour days in a cotton mill by eleven. Police arrested the sisters on the Exposition Cotton Mill picket line in September 1934. They were held at Fulton Tower Prison under $5,000 bail each, accused of circulating insurrectionary literature under the statute used against Angelo Herndon. International Labor Defense attorney John Geer represented them at a bail-reduction hearing; attorney Louis Tatham also worked on their defense. Young described eviction from mill housing and the loss of her furniture while supporting her children and unemployed husband. Both sisters were out on bond by June 1936, with the charges still pending.

operations.research_note: Primary autobiographical pamphlet identifies Leah/Nanny Washburn and explicitly marks May 3, 1975 as 75th birthday; confirms May 3, 1900. Contemporary Atlanta Daily World names Assistant Solicitor John Hudson. Secondary obituary citation gives May 1, 1996, held pending direct obituary; 74 days reported secondary, not proposed without original.

operations.name: Bruce Stevens Proctor

expected.name: Bruce Stevens Proctor
expected.description: Bruce Stevens Proctor was a Defense Intelligence Agency employee who examined reconnaissance photographs from Southeast Asia and concluded that the U.S. government was bombing civilian villages while publicly denying it. He resigned from the DIA and joined the Air National Guard to avoid the draft, but his unit was activated for Vietnam. In 1968 he went absent without leave rather than participate in a war he considered immoral and sought refuge in Sweden. Proctor lived there as an American war exile for four years, then immigrated to Canada in 1972. He remained in Winnipeg, worked in education and public service and died there in 2011.

operations.name: Hisashi Fukuhara

expected.name: Hisashi Fukuhara
expected.description: Hisashi Fukuhara was an Issei barber-shop owner from Honokaa, Hawaii, who assisted local residents with the Japanese Consulate. JCCH records his birth year as 1897 and the pen name Fukuhara Getsugaku. His own record lists Kilauea Military Camp before Sand Island. His individual timeline documents arrest in December 1941, mainland transfer March 1942, Angel Island March-April 1942, Fort Sill April-May 1942, Camp Livingston June 1942-June 1943, Fort Missoula June 1943-April 1944 and Santa Fe April 1944-October 1945. He returned to Hawaii aboard Yarmouth in November 1945. This was administrative US wartime civilian detention in the context of Japanese ancestry and community roles. No individual criminal conviction or judicial sentence is established; exact arrest and release days are not documented. Source: https://incarceration.jcchawaii.org/internees/fukuhara-hisashi-getsugaku
